lead: A planar gate controls the channel from above only. Once the channel is short, that grip is too weak, and the usual fixes — thinner oxide, heavier doping — raise leakage faster than they help. A FinFET lifts the channel into a thin vertical silicon fin and wraps the gate over the top and both sides. Control returns without an impossibly thin oxide. FinFETs became the standard transistor of advanced logic from the 22 nm node.
prereq: You need: 1.6 for short-channel effects and 1.7 for the leakage they cause.

blocks.text: In a planar MOSFET the gate sits on top of a flat channel and controls it from one side. The drain also pulls on the channel, and its share grows as L falls (see 1.6). The standard fixes make things worse. A thinner oxide leaks by tunnelling. Heavier body doping raises junction leakage and junction capacitance and cuts mobility. It does shrink the depletion widths, so it helps contain the drain field, but it stops working once the body must be thin.

The real fix is a thinner body. If the silicon under the gate is thinner than the depletion width it would otherwise need, it is fully depleted even at zero gate bias. Almost no mobile charge is left for the drain to steal, and the gate field reaches the whole body. Control comes from geometry instead of a thinner oxide (1.7).

sections.h3: The fin and its effective width

blocks.text: The fin is a narrow ridge of silicon etched from the wafer. Its width is Wfin (nm) and its height is Hfin (nm). Gate oxide and gate metal cover the top and both sides — a tri-gate. A double-gate version covers only the two sides.

blocks.where: Weff is the effective channel width of one fin in nm; Hfin is the fin height in nm, counted twice for the two sidewalls; Wfin is the fin width in nm, the top surface. A pure double gate gives Weff = 2Hfin.

blocks.text: Because the body is thin, the channel is undoped or lightly doped. Threshold voltage is set by the gate work function — the energy needed to pull an electron out of the gate metal, in eV — and by Wfin, not by body doping. There is little body effect and less impurity scattering. Trade-offs: Wfin must stay well below the gate length to remain fully depleted, Hfin sets current per fin, and tall thin fins are hard to pattern and can bend.

A planar designer draws any W. A FinFET designer chooses a whole number of fins in parallel, so drive strength snaps to fin counts and cells are drawn on a fin pitch — the centre-to-centre distance between neighbouring fins, in nm. Threshold is tuned by work function, drive by fin count. Gate-all-around surrounds a stacked horizontal nanosheet on all four sides, so a wider body gives the same control and more current per unit area.

figure.caption: Control moves from one side to a wrapped gate. Each step gives the gate more surface over a thinner body, which restores authority over a short channel.

spec.title: Gate control from one side to four
spec.aria: A progression from a planar gate through a thin fully depleted body to a fin with the gate on three sides and then a gate wrapped all the way around the channel.

examples.question: A FinFET has Wfin = 10 nm and Hfin = 30 nm. (a) Find Weff per fin. (b) How many fins give 700 nm of drive width? (c) At 1 mA per µm, find the current per fin and the cell total.
steps: 70 nm = 0.07 µm, so current per fin = 0.07 × 1 mA/µm = 70 µA.
examples.answer: Weff = 70 nm, 10 fins, 70 µA per fin, 0.7 mA total.
examples.check:
Wfin = 10.0
Hfin = 30.0
Weff = 2 * Hfin + Wfin
print(Weff)
Wneed = 700.0
nfins = int(Wneed / Weff)
print(nfins)
Iper_fin_uA = (Weff / 1000.0) * 1.0 * 1000.0
print(Iper_fin_uA)
print(nfins * Iper_fin_uA / 1000.0)

traps: Using Wfin alone as the effective width. With Wfin = 10 nm and Hfin = 30 nm that under-counts drive seven times.
Forgetting width quantisation. A request for 720 nm needs 11 fins (770 nm), not 10.3 fins.
Saying the FinFET removes short-channel effects. It reduces them; drain-induced barrier lowering still exists.
Mixing formulas: a double-gate fin gives Weff = 2Hfin, a tri-gate fin gives 2Hfin + Wfin.

quiz.q: Define Wfin, Hfin and Weff for a tri-gate fin.
quiz.a: Wfin is the fin width in nm, Hfin the fin height in nm, and Weff = 2Hfin + Wfin is the effective width of one fin in nm.

quiz.q: What sets the threshold voltage of a FinFET?
quiz.a: The gate work function and the fin width Wfin, not body doping, because the body is undoped or lightly doped.

quiz.q: Why does a thin fully depleted body reduce the drain's control of the channel?
quiz.a: In a thin fully depleted body the gate is very close to every part of the channel, so most drain field lines end on the gate instead of on the body. The drain shifts little charge, the source barrier stays fixed, and drain-induced barrier lowering is small.

quiz.q: A fin has Wfin = 8 nm and Hfin = 25 nm. Find Weff and the number of fins needed for 580 nm of drive width.
If one fin carries 58 µA, how many fins give at least 0.6 mA?
quiz.a: 600 µA ÷ 58 µA = 10.3, rounded up to 11 fins, since only whole fins exist. Eleven fins give 638 µA.

quiz.q: For the same L and the same drive current, why does a FinFET cell leak less than a planar cell?
quiz.a: The gate wraps three sides of a thin, lightly doped body, giving a steeper subthreshold slope and a lower off-current at the same threshold. Short-channel effects are reduced, not eliminated.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production logic at the smallest nodes has moved to gate-all-around nanosheets, with the gate surrounding stacked horizontal channels. Research is on forksheet and stacked complementary FETs that pair nMOS and pMOS vertically to cut cell area. FinFETs remain the mainstream transistor in most shipped chips and in most teaching flows.
